summary: Provides guidance on collaboration between the ITU-T and the Internet Engineering Task Force on developing standards. It updates and obsoletes RFC 3356. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6756 gives the IETF and ITU-T ways to stay informed about standards work that may overlap. It recommends early contact, regular review of new work, and clear procedures for exchanging documents.

questions: how do ietf and itu-t collaborate
what is the ietf new-work mailing list
subtitle: Guidance for the IETF and ITU-T to coordinate standards work.

tldr.problem: The IETF and ITU-T develop standards through different processes, so work that overlaps or depends on the other body can be missed without early communication.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends identifying contact points, monitoring each other's work, sharing drafts, and using liaison statements for formal communication.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6756 is Informational, obsoletes RFC 3356, and has been updated by RFC 9141. It is guidance, not a protocol standard.

today: RFC 6756 obsoletes RFC 3356 and is updated by RFC 9141. It is an Informational document that provides collaboration guidance.

sections.title: Why the Organizations Coordinate
sections.content:
This RFC provides non-normative guidance for cooperation between the International Telecommunication Union Telecommunication Standardization Sector (ITU-T) and the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF). Its goal is to identify topics of mutual interest early and support constructive work.

The organizations have different structures. IETF work is organized in working groups and is mostly conducted on public mailing lists; ITU-T work is organized around study Questions and meetings led by rapporteurs. The RFC recommends contact points such as an ITU-T study group chairman and an IETF area director.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF and ITU-T organize their work differently, so each needs people who know whom to contact in the other organization. Early contact helps them notice related work before it becomes a surprise.

sections.title: Tracking Existing and Proposed Work
sections.content:
ITU-T study groups should review IETF working-group charters and active Internet-Drafts, then contact the relevant chair and area director when they find common work. IETF participants can review ITU-T study-group Questions and work programmes and contact the relevant leadership.

The IETF sends draft charters for new or revised working groups and Birds-of-a-Feather announcements to its new-work mailing list. ITU-T representatives can monitor that list; study groups can also notify the list when they draft or create new Questions. The RFC notes that an IETF charter process can take as little as two weeks.
sections.plainLanguage: Each organization checks the other's active work and alerts the right contacts about possible overlap. A shared mailing list helps reveal proposed work while it is still being planned.

sections.title: Representation and Formal Communication
sections.content:
Experts chosen by IETF leadership normally participate in ITU-T meetings as Internet Society (ISOC) delegates. An ITU-T study group chairman may authorize members to attend an IETF meeting as ITU-T delegates; their opinions receive the same weight as those of other working-group participants.

Experts are encouraged to communicate informally. Formal messages from an ITU-T body must be approved and identified as coming from that body, and liaison statements follow the procedures in RFC 4053. IETF mailing lists are open to subscribers; access to ITU-T lists has different membership conditions.
sections.plainLanguage: Participants can attend meetings on behalf of the other organization under its procedures. Formal statements must clearly show that they represent an organization, rather than an individual's view.

sections.title: Sharing Drafts and Referencing Standards
sections.content:
The organizations can exchange drafts by email, URLs or formal liaison statements. RFC 6756 discourages proprietary-format attachments on IETF mailing lists and says official IETF documents are in ASCII.

The recommended result is for one organization to document work fully and the other to reference that document. The RFC discourages joint text because the two organizations have different approval and revision procedures. It also describes focus groups and Birds-of-a-Feather sessions as ways to discuss possible work before formal groups begin.
sections.plainLanguage: The organizations can share drafts and ask each other to review them. The RFC recommends that one body write the full specification and the other reference it.

sections.title: Security and Changes Since RFC 3356
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section says that cooperation procedures have no direct Internet security implications. The document is an informational guide and defines no network protocol.

RFC 6756 updates and obsoletes RFC 3356. Its changes include updated liaison procedures and information about early work efforts such as ITU-T focus groups and IETF Birds-of-a-Feather sessions.
sections.plainLanguage: This document describes how organizations cooperate, not how network traffic is secured. It replaces an earlier collaboration guide and updates its procedures.
